event.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
event.description:
Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools.

Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other. This exhibition inhabits that intersection, where historic technologies of encoding meet their digital descendants. Printmaking and weaving become contact zones between traditional craft techniques and computational processes, recording and recoding gestures across media: photographs compressed and reassembled as strips, atomized prints woven into textile, and thrown clay fused with digitally printed forms. 

Where does resistance live in a material, and how do we encounter it? How do different materials choreograph their maker’s creative gestures through this resistance? As creative workflows migrate into digital space, something of that friction transforms. Tangling the Digital asks what becomes possible when that resistance is embraced rather than engineered away. 
A working loom lives in the gallery, bearing witness to the evolution of craft as weavings unfurl over the course of the exhibition. 

Together, the works invite visitors to locate the human body—as maker, as observer—in what they see.

event.title: Evolving Approaches to Open Science and Research Transparency Education (Bay Area Open Science Group Meeting)
event.description:
This month we are joined by Jo Weech, Research Transparency Program Manager at the Berkeley Initiative for Transparency in the Social Sciences BITSS. Jo supports teams working on academic forecasting, evidence aggregation, and reporting in economics. In addition to its research projects, BITSS hosts an annual conference and course on research transparency. Her presentation for the September meeting will be on how education in open science and research transparency has evolved due to changes in researcher norms and use of AI.

About the Bay Area Open Science Group
The Bay Area Open Science Group is a growing community for Bay Area academics and researchers interested in incorporating open science into their research, teaching, and learning. Targeting students, faculty, and staff at UCSF, Berkeley, and Stanford, the goal of the community is to increase awareness of and engagement with all things open science, including open access articles, open research data, open source software, and open educational resources. Through this work the group hopes to connect researchers with tools they can use to make the products and process of science more equitable and reproducible.

event.title: Applied Physics/Physics Colloquium: Benjamin Safdi - " The Search for Axion Dark Matter"
event.description:
Abstract: Axions are some of the best-motivated beyond the Standard Model particle candidates at present. These ultralight particles may account for the cosmological dark matter and explain other outstanding problems in nature, such as the strong-CP problem; they also are now known to emerge generically in string theory. Axions are expected to couple ultra-weakly with ordinary matter, which complicates their detection. However, thanks to recent theoretical, experimental, and observational progress these particles may be discovered or ruled out within the near future. I will review some of the recent ideas that may soon play a role in axion discovery, including theoretical predictions for the axion mass and novel observational signatures of axions that emerge in extreme astrophysical environments such as supernovae.

Benjamin Safdi received his undergraduate degree from the University of Colorado at Boulder, a Master of Advanced Study from Cambridge University, as a Churchill Scholar, and his PhD from Princeton University in 2014. He was then a Pappalardo Fellow at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology until 2017, when he started as an assistant professor at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. Dr. Safdi moved to LBNL in 2020 and then to UC Berkeley in 2021. He received the Department of Energy Early Career Award in 2018, the IUPAP C11 Young Scientist Prize in Particles and Fields in 2020, the Sloan Research Fellowship in 2023, and the New Horizons in Physics Prize in 2026 for his contributions to the search for the axion.

event.title: Georgian Cinema Now: Temo Re (2025)
event.description:
Georgian cinema is experiencing a remarkable renaissance. Over the past fifteen years, filmmakers from Georgia have earned acclaim at major international festivals, including the Berlinale, Karlovy Vary, Locarno, and IDFA (Amsterdam). This creative flourishing, however, exists in stark contrast to the increasingly repressive political environment in Georgia since the ascent of an authoritarian government in 2024. Independent filmmakers now face severe threats to their freedom of expression and the basic conditions necessary for financing, producing, and exhibiting films domestically, including those perceived as critical of the government.

Georgian Cinema Now will be presented in installments over the course of the coming year, offering an unprecedented opportunity to experience the power, artistry, and urgency of contemporary Georgian filmmaking at a time when it is most at risk. Through screenings, conversations, scholarship, and international collaboration, the project will deepen public understanding of Georgia’s cultural landscape and highlight the essential role of independent artists in societies where democratic freedoms are threatened. A delegation of ten filmmakers and experts will visit the San Francisco Bay Area for ten days in late September, creating a festival-like launch for this ongoing retrospective.

—Susan Oxtoby, Director of Film and Senior Film Curator
Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA)

Temo Re
Anka Gujabidze (Georgia, 2025)

Salomé Asatiani is a journalist and podcast host at Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Georgian Service and co-screenwriter of Temo Re. 
 
With Temo Re, photographer and filmmaker Anka Gujabidze creates a multifaceted portrait of Georgia’s capital city, Tbilisi. event.title: Cotton and State Power in China: The First Hundred Years
event.description:
In a 1929 survey of global cloth consumption, China was near the bottom: only four countries consumed less cloth per capita than China, and three of these were in sub-Saharan Africa. China with its dense population and limited agricultural land was unable to clothe itself. Almost one hundred years later, China is the world’s main producer, main exporter, and main consumer of textiles and garments: in 2020: 64 percent of the world’s yarn, 60 percent of its fabric, and 35 percent of its garments were produced in China. China’s rise to the status of textile superpower did not start, as is often assumed, in the reform era: already by 1952, China was a net exporter of cotton cloth; by 1967, it surpassed Japan as the world’s largest exporter of textiles. This talk traces China’s textile industry through five stages: (1) the standardization and scaling-up of cotton cultivation beginning in the 1930s, (2) the evolution of a brutally extractive system in the Mao years that mobilized rural labor for cotton cultivation while rationing cloth supplies below subsistence needs, (3) the transition from a muscle-powered to a fossil fuel energy regime in the late Mao years, and the parallel development of a synthetic fiber industry, (4) the abandonment of Mao-era textile towns in inland China and the construction of a new export-oriented textile industry in coastal China, and (5) the ecologically and politically risky move of cotton cultivation from the old inland districts to Xinjiang, now home to 90 percent of China’s cotton output.

This event is open to the public. Please RSVP here. 

About the speaker:

Jacob Eyferth is a social historian of China with research interests in the life and work experience of nonelite people throughout the twentieth century. Trained at the universities of Berlin and Leiden, he has held postdoctoral fellowships at Oxford, Harvard, and Rutgers and taught at Simon Fraser University. Currently, he is associate professor in the department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations of the University of Chicago. Most of his work has focused on the countryside and on the mid-twentieth century, c. 1920–1970. His first book, Eating Rice from Bamboo Roots, is an ethnographic history of a community of rural papermakers in Sichuan. It won the 2011 Joseph Levenson Prize for the best book on China in the post-1900 category. He is currently working on a second book, tentatively titled Cotton, Gender, and Revolution in Twentieth-Century China, that uses cloth and clothing as a lens through which to analyze how the monumental changes of the twentieth century—revolution, collectivization, industrialization, etc.—transformed the lives of rural women.

In Conversation: Elene Naveriani

Blackbird Blackbird Blackberry
Elene Naveriani (Georgia/Switzerland, 2023)

(Shashvi shashvi maq’vali). Based on feminist writer Tamta Melashvili’s celebrated novel, this gem of a film follows Etero (Eka Chavleishvili), a forty-eight-year-old woman who lives happily in a provincial Georgian village. The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future.

The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist.

The exhibition is curated by Jee-Young Park, Korean Studies Librarian, and Jisoo Kim, an SFSU MA Museum Studies graduate and San Francisco-based curator.

event.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
event.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition.

event.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
event.room_number: Bowes Art & Architecture Library, 2nd floor. Visitors: Please call 650-723-3408 for building/elevator access.
event.description:
Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet.

Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm.

event.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
event.description:
Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. 

Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century.  If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. 

Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. 

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970, acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. The exhibit highlights the city’s rapid changes and their diverse causes, while suggesting the collection’s vast possibilities for both research and instruction.

This exhibition is curated by Sarah Sussman, Assistant University Librarian for Collections and Services & Curator of French and Italian Collections, Stanford University Libraries, and Chloe Summers Edmondson, Assistant Professor of French at the University of Miami. Produced and designed by Deardra Fuzzell, with assistance from Kylee Jo Diedrich, Sofia McGullam Ornelas, and Pasha Tope.

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford will be open to the public. Registration at the entrance with a valid government ID is required to enter the Cecil H. Green Library and view the exhibit.

event.title: Updates in the Management of Primary Biliary Cholangitis
event.description:
Overview
This activity reviews current, evidence-based management of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC): diagnosis and confirmatory testing, baseline risk stratification and staging, treatment targets and assessment of response to ursodeoxycholic acid, second-line PPAR agonist therapy with seladelpar and elafibranor, and management of pruritus, fatigue, and other extrahepatic manifestations. Through case-based audience polling and expert review of recent trial data, participants will be prepared to identify high-risk patients earlier and intensify therapy to improve long-term outcomes.

Registration

Registration for all practitioners - free.

To register for this activity, please click HERE

Credits

AMA PRA Category 1 Credits™ (1.00 hours), AAPA Category 1 CME credits (1.00 hours), ANCC Contact Hours (1.00 hours), Non-Physician Participation Credit (1.00 hours)

Target Audience
Specialties - Family Medicine & Community Health, Gastroenterology, Gastroenterology & Hepatology, Internal Medicine, Primary Care & Population Health
Professions - Advance Practice Nurse (APN), Non-Physician, Physician, Physician Associate, Registered Nurse (RN)
 
Objectives
At the conclusion of this activity, learners should be able to:


1. Apply diagnostic criteria for PBC, including anti-gp210 and anti-sp100 testing in AMA-negative patients, and initiate ursodeoxycholic acid 13-15 mg/kg/day.
2. Utilize VCTE or MRE and prognostic scores (GLOBE and UK-PBC) to risk-stratify patients at baseline and guide disease staging and surveillance intervals.
3. Assess biochemical response to first-line therapy at the appropriate interval — 6 months in high-risk patients — using ALP and total bilirubin thresholds.
4. Evaluate the efficacy and safety data for seladelpar and elafibranor and select second-line therapy for inadequate UDCA responders.
5. Review and manage extrahepatic manifestations of PBC, including pruritus (including linerixibat), fatigue, and sicca symptoms.

Accreditation

In support of improving patient care, Stanford Medicine is jointly accredited by the Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education (ACCME), the Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education (ACPE), and the American Nurses Credentialing Center (ANCC), to provide continuing education for the healthcare team.

American Medical Association (AMA) 
Stanford Medicine designates this Live Activity for a maximum of 1.00 AMA PRA Category 1 CreditsTM.  Physicians should claim only the credit commensurate with the extent of their participation in the activity. 

American Nurses Credentialing Center (ANCC) 
Stanford Medicine designates this Live Activity for a maximum of 1.00 ANCC contact hours.  

American Academy of Physician Associates (AAPA) - Live 
Stanford Medicine has been authorized by the American Academy of PAs (AAPA) to award AAPA Category 1 CME credit for activities planned in accordance with AAPA CME Criteria. This live activity is designated for 1.00 AAPA Category 1 CME credits. PAs should only claim credit commensurate with the extent of their participation.

This activity reviews current, evidence-based management of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC): diagnosis and confirmatory testing, baseline risk stratification and staging, treatment targets and assessment of response to ursodeoxycholic acid, second-line PPAR agonist therapy with seladelpar and elafibranor, and management of pruritus, fatigue, and other extrahepatic manifestations. Through case-based audience polling and expert review of recent trial data, participants will be prepared to identify high-risk patients earlier and intensify therapy to improve long-term outcomes.

event.title: Chasing Freedom: Coming of Age at the End of Empire - Dr. Simukai Chigudu
event.description:
Session Description: 

Join Dr. Simukai Chigudu for a book talk on Chasing Freedom: a story of being born in postcolonial Zimbabwe, shaped by his family's buried trauma of war and liberation. It is a moving account of a generation still searching for the freedom they were promised. 

Dr. Simukai Chigudu’s Chasing Freedom: Coming of Age at the End of Empire is a candid, emotionally resonant exploration of family, nation, and the promises and limits of liberation. Drawing on his own life, Dr. Chigudu reconstructs a family shaped by struggle: a grandfather killed by the Rhodesian regime, a father who endured imprisonment and later fought as a guerrilla, and a mother who broke social constraints to support other women. Yet his upbringing was also suffused with British cultural practices, singing English folk songs, reading Shakespeare, and playing cricket, setting the stage for a disorienting culture shock when, in 2002, he left Zimbabwe for a boarding school in northern England. The book traces how historical violence, migration, and education reconfigure identity and belonging, and how a new generation continues to seek the freedom imagined by earlier movements. With scholarly rigor and humane storytelling, Dr. Chigudu offers a moving account of inherited trauma, resilience, and the complex legacies of empire, prompting reflection on both personal healing and public memory. 

About the Speaker

Simukai Chigudu is an associate professor of African politics at the University of Oxford and a fellow of St Antony’s College. He was previously a fellow at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences at Stanford University. His academic monograph, The Political Life of an Epidemic: Cholera, Crisis and Citizenship in Zimbabwe (Cambridge University Press, 2020), received the 2021 APSA-IPSA Theodore J. Lowi First Book Award. He holds a DPhil in International Development from the University of Oxford, and his doctoral thesis received the 2018 Audrey Richards Prize, a biennial award presented by the African Studies Association of the United Kingdom for the best doctoral thesis in African Studies examined at a UK institution. Before entering academia, he worked as a medical doctor in the NHS for three years. He was also one of the founding members of Rhodes Must Fall in Oxford, and has become a leading voice in public debates on the cultural politics of colonialism and racism. Chasing Freedom is his first trade book.

event.title: CMEMS: Reviel Netz presents, "The Shaping of Modern Science"
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 260, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
Organized and hosted by the Center for Medieval and Early Modern Studies (CMEMS).

Reviel Netz (Classics, Stanford) presents, "The Shaping of Modern Science: Paper Practices in the 17th Century"

Event Sponsor: Program in History and Philosophy of Science

With a response from Yoav Levinson-Sela (History, Stanford). See the abstract below.

Koyré, discovering that Galileo and Descartes both moved in parallel towards the discovery of the law of free fall – but that only Galileo made it – used this to identify Galileo’s originality as the first to form the specifically dynamic concepts of modern physics. The more recent realization - that Thomas Harriot, too, made the same discovery as Galileo, following a similar path, and a similarly protracted campaign – should help us see the historical originality not in terms of shared concepts, but instead of shared practices. Everyone involved – Descartes, Galileo, Harriot – pursued protracted campaigns based on curating paper archives for which there were no ancient or medieval antecedents. The thesis proposed by the talk, then, is bold: that modern science was shaped by its new paper practices.

event.title: Masua Sagiv — Israel's 2026 Elections: Make or Break?
event.description:
On October 27, 2026, Israelis will vote in national elections widely seen as perhaps the most consequential in the country's modern history. Why do Israelis view the 2026 elections in such dramatic, even existential, terms? Who are the main contenders and what are the main issues on which Israel will vote in the first national elections since the October 7, 2023 attack and subsequent wars? And what are the possible scenarios for the outcome of the elections? Join Amichai Magen and Masua Sagiv in conversation about these questions.

ABOUT THE SPEAKER:

Dr. Masua Sagiv is a Senior Faculty member of the Shalom Hartman Institute and the academic advisor of its Center for Shared Society, as well as a senior fellow at the Helen Diller Institute, U.C. Berkeley. Masua’s work addresses the fundamental challenges facing both Israeli society and North American Jewish communities, from rising antisemitism and campus tensions to Jewish peoplehood and the complex relationship between Israel and world Jewry. Masua’s scholarly work focuses on the development of contemporary Judaism in Israel, as a culture, religion, nationality, and as part of Israel’s identity as a Jewish and democratic state. Her research explores the role of law, state actors, and civil society organizations in promoting social change across diverse issues: shared society, religion and gender, religion and state, and Jewish peoplehood.

Masua recently returned to Israel after four years in Berkeley, California, where she was a senior faculty member for the Shalom Hartman Institute of North America and the Koret Visiting Assistant Professor at the Helen Diller Institute at UC Berkeley. Prior to her tenure in the Bay Area, Masua was the Academic Director of the Menomadin Center for Jewish and Democratic Law at Bar-Ilan University and taught at the Schools of Law at Bar-Ilan University and Tel-Aviv University. She co-led a leadership program for high-school students, for which she received the Israeli Hope in Academia Prize from former Israeli President Reuven Rivlin, and was awarded the Gorney Prize for Young Scholar in Public Law. Her book, Radical Conservativism (in Hebrew), on the Halachic Feminist struggle in Israel, was published by Carmel Publishing House in 2024.

event.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Ryushi Miyayama - "Atmospheric chemical evolution driven by meteoritic interactions"
event.stream_info: Email Jeremy Samos (samosj@stanford.edu) for the Zoom meeting information
event.description:
Planetary atmospheres - and their potential habitability - evolve under external energy inputs, including stellar irradiation, cosmic rays, and meteoroid accretion. Meteoroid entry is ubiquitous across planetary systems but its role as a driver of atmospheric chemical evolution remains relatively underexplored. Meteorites readily acquire high entry velocities through planetary gravitational focusing, generating strong shock waves in planetary atmospheres during the entry process. The resulting shock heating drives non-equilibrium chemical reactions that can alter atmospheric compositions. We investigate these processes using coupled aerodynamical and chemical kinetic simulations of meteoroid entry. Our results demonstrate that meteoritic heating can significantly contribute to the production of organic species. Compared with other external energy sources such as stellar irradiation and cosmic rays, meteoroid entry processes have received relatively limited attention in atmospheric chemistry studies. Our results suggest that unlike stellar irradiation, which is primarily absorbed in the upper atmosphere, meteoroids can directly deposit energy into deeper atmospheric layers where most of the atmospheric mass resides. This enables shock-induced chemistry to proceed efficiently in dense atmospheric regions. Therefore, meteoritic heating may be a major contributor to chemical production in planetary atmospheres.

Dr. Ryushi Miyayama is a postdoctoral scholar in Earth and Planetary Sciences under the supervision of Prof. Laura Schaefer. He received his Ph.D. in Physics from Nagoya University in 2026. During his Ph.D., he also worked with Prof. Schaefer on the physics and chemistry of planetary atmospheres, particularly how impacts and meteoroid entry drive atmospheric evolution. His recent work investigates shock-driven nonequilibrium chemistry during meteoroid entry into Titan’s atmosphere and its implications for the production of prebiotic molecules.

 

Suggested reading: Ryushi Miyayama et al 2025 ApJ 989 210, https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/1538-4357/adf064

event.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
event.description:
Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools.

Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other. This exhibition inhabits that intersection, where historic technologies of encoding meet their digital descendants. Printmaking and weaving become contact zones between traditional craft techniques and computational processes, recording and recoding gestures across media: photographs compressed and reassembled as strips, atomized prints woven into textile, and thrown clay fused with digitally printed forms. 

Where does resistance live in a material, and how do we encounter it? How do different materials choreograph their maker’s creative gestures through this resistance? As creative workflows migrate into digital space, something of that friction transforms. Tangling the Digital asks what becomes possible when that resistance is embraced rather than engineered away. 
A working loom lives in the gallery, bearing witness to the evolution of craft as weavings unfurl over the course of the exhibition. 

Together, the works invite visitors to locate the human body—as maker, as observer—in what they see.

event.title: Emergent Properties: Decennial Reflections on Collections
event.description:
In 2026 the David Rumsey Map Center celebrates its tenth year—a moment to reflect on how the Center has added value to scholarship on campus and around the world. event.title: Conversations on Korean Modern and Contemporary Art
event.description:
Join us for Conversations on Modern and Contemporary Art of Korea, a symposium bridging generations of contemporary Korean art. This event spotlights two groundbreaking artists: Yun Hyong-keun (1928–2007), a pioneering figure of the Dansaekhwa monochromatic painting movement, and contemporary artist Wonwoo Lee, whose thought-provoking installations, sculptures, and performances reinterpret everyday life with humor and irony.

Hyoeun Kim, Assistant Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA, will introduce the two speakers: POSTECH professor Jung-Ah Woo, who will speak about the evolution of Korean modern and contemporary art; and Wonwoo Lee, who will discuss his own work. The two lectures will be followed by a moderated Q&A session with Dafna Zur, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages and Cultures at Stanford University.

(Image: [Top half]  Portrait of Yun Hyong-keun Yun Hyong-keun at his studio, late 1980s © Yun Seong-ryeol. Courtesy of PKM Gallery. [Bottom half] Wonwoo Lee, courtesy of Artist / Photo by Iean Yang <양이언>)

This event is free and open to the public. Please RSVP Here. 

About the speakers:

Jung-Ah Woo, is Professor and Head of the Division of Humanities and Social Sciences at POSTECH (Pohang University of Science and Technology), South Korea, where she also serves as Director of the POSTECH Future Intellectuals Academy. Woo’s research focuses on the conceptual development of contemporary Korean art and its relationship to global contemporaneity. Her most recent book, The Conceptual Turn and the Origins of Contemporaneity in Korean Art (Somyong Publishing, 2022) explores these research topics. A prolific public scholar, she has been a weekly art columnist for The Chosun Ilbo since 2011 and is a board member of the Samsung Foundation of Culture. Woo holds a Ph.D. in Art History from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and was a Getty Scholar at the Getty Research Institute in Los Angeles (2018–2019).

Wonwoo Lee reinterprets fragments from everyday lives through his unique sense of humor and wit, thus interrupting everyday routine and revitalizing mundane subject matters. The imagination that giants cast away anxiety, symbols of luck (clovers, stars, rainbows), trivial conversations, and objects of distorted shapes and meanings work as self-defensive jokes and a sign of warning towards the banal world. Lee is a versatile artist who works across a variety of genres including performance, sculpture, paintings, photography, video, and text. He is a member of ‘…Joketta Project’ and 'MLH,' a multi-genre group. He has been actively exhibiting works at various museums including Seoul Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), Art Sonje Center (Seoul, Korea), Amore Pacific Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), and Songzhuang Art Gallery (Beijing, China), and has gained significant attention from both local and international curators, critics, collectors, and related art professionals.

event.title: Sensing Nankeen: Skilled Perception as an Alternative to Centralized Production
event.description:
Join the Fiber Optics Research Workshop in welcoming Professor Jacob Eyferth (University of Chicago) to Stanford Campus. Professor Eyferth will give a presentation entitled 'Sensing Nankeen: Skilled Perception as an Alternative to Centralized Production.'

The Jiangnan cotton industry, centered on Songjiang (today part of Shanghai), was one of the largest industries of the eighteenth century in terms of volume and employment. Jiangnan cotton cloth, known in Europe as nankeen, was produced in millions of small household workshops and collected by traveling merchants who toured the countryside by boat and bought cloth in small batches, for further processing in urban workshops. Buying cloth required sensory skills: as Qianlong-periond training manuals explain, a skilled “cloth viewer” had to be able to assess the quality – the weight, density, color, etc. – of a bolt of cloth at first sight; moreover, he would know, by viewing and touching it, where, when, and how it was produced, with what tools, and from what raw materials. Most importantly, he could predict how the cloth would change under the dyers’ hands: cloth that looked smooth and clean might turn into stiff like felt in the vat, while cloth that looked less impressive would gain luster. Rather than seeking to standardize production, Songjiang cloth merchants embraced variety: all cloth, good or bad, had its use; even the coarsest cloth would find a market. The merchant’s task was to match product to market, using his body as scale and yardstick.  The talk reconstructs cloth viewers’ embodied techniques as described in the Bu Jing 布经 training manual, asks to which extend skilled vision was, or could have been, an alternative to standardization and mass production, and looks at sensory training in Mao-era textile factories.

This event is sponsored by Fiber Optics: Plant Fiber Materials & Media, a Research Workshop hosted by the Stanford Humanities Center, with support from the Center for East Asian Studies.

event.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
event.description:
Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material.

Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions. Institutional Seat (2022) modifies a standard bench from the museum’s galleries into a version that is more comfortable for all museum visitors. Surround Sound (2022) attends to the floor of the gallery with dance-floor materials. Over the course of the exhibition, this floor will collect marks made by visitors’ shoes, strollers, and wheelchair treads, like another form of tally or notation.

Carolyn Lazard (b. 1987) is a New York-based artist whose primary medium is iteration. They also work across video, sculpture, installation, and performance. Their practice remembers the generative incapacity of debility.

Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is organized by the Cantor Arts Center, presenting work originally co-commissioned by the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis; the Institute of Contemporary Art, University of Pennsylvania; and Nottingham Contemporary, and is curated by Christina Linden, Director of Academic and Public Programs. We gratefully acknowledge support from The Lynn Krywick Gibbons Gallery Exhibitions Fund at the Cantor Arts Center.

event.description:
The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future.

The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist.

The exhibition is curated by Jee-Young Park, Korean Studies Librarian, and Jisoo Kim, an SFSU MA Museum Studies graduate and San Francisco-based curator.

event.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
event.description:
Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. An accompanying catalogue features four newly commissioned essays accompanied by previously unpublished documentation, deepening our understanding of this overlooked chapter in the history of art and technology.

Image: François Willème (French, 1830–1905). Unfinished photosculpture bust, ca. 1860. Oak and twine on base. Gift of Eastman Kodak Company, ex-collection Gabriel Cromer, 1985.0517.0001. Courtesy of the George Eastman Museum

event.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition.

Did you know that advisors from Fidelity Investments and TIAA provide free individual financial counseling on campus at your convenience? They can offer guidance on the best strategy to meet your retirement goals through Stanford's retirement savings plans.

Contact Fidelity directly to schedule an appointment with a representative to review your current and future retirement savings options:

  • Fidelity appointment scheduler
  • (800) 642-7131
